# Introduction

Why do political parties decide to (de)centralize their campaigns?
Party leaders face an important information challenge: it is not possible
for one single person to know about all the local issues of every single
district.  Furthermore, they need to be concerned about national issues,
which can be partially related to local ones. In this situation, and
when seeking reelection, they need to decide how much they
want to campaign on a national platform, or whether they want to leave some
discretionary power to their candidates. Leaving this room can allow
candidates to tailor their campaigns to the local issues of each district,
which can lead to better electoral outcomes. This project explores this
question using the case of Japan. It introduces a new dataset
built from electoral bulletins, as well as new measures of party
centralization.  We begin by reviewing previous work on delegation
and decentralization in single-member district electoral systems. Then,
we introduce the model of this paper. The following sections present
the dataset, the pipeline, and preliminary results. Finally, we lay out
the deliverables for the next steps.

# Theory {#sec-theory}

## Literature {#sec-literature}

Why do political parties decide to (de)centralize their political
campaigns? Arguably, the answer to this question depends on many factors,
most importantly the structures under which elections take
place. Rather than trying to find an answer that would be applicable to
every electoral system, political system, and state structure (federal
vs. unitary), we focus on parliamentary single-member district
(SMD) systems.  The argument concerns national-level elections; therefore, it
might not extend to subnational elections.

These initial scope conditions are also justified by the existing
literature. Previous research has highlighted that, as political and
economic power lies at different levels in federal versus unitary states,
these structures change how parties and voters make their strategic choices
[@chhibber_etal04; @mendozagomez26].

Why do parties (de)centralize campaigns? Some previous explanations focused
on the incentives of candidates to cultivate a personal reputation that
is distinct from the party's reputation [@carey_shugart95]. While this account
situates the candidate as the decision-maker, rather than the
party deciding how much discretion candidates can have, some elements are
useful for thinking about this question. Among the most important factors
is the electoral system, as it shapes the control party leaders have over
the ballot, how pooled the votes are, and how votes are allocated. In
the case of interest here, SMD, personal reputation is the least
important.

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item[\textbf{H1}]: Individual candidates' bulletins are aligned with the
party (little discretionary power).
\end{itemize}
```

However, while informative about the strategic choices of candidates
in SMD systems, this prediction does not seem adequate. A key
feature of Japanese politics is the centrality of personal support networks known as
Kōenkai. Therefore, it is unrealistic to expect personal ties to have
little to no effect on campaigns in Japan. Accounts of the LDP's historic
loss in 2009 highlight the role of party centralization
and cutbacks in particularistic spending, which was the core of the
clientelistic foundation of the LDP's electoral dominance [@reed_etal12;
@scheiner06]. While @reed_etal12 predict that the shift toward a
less discretionary and more nationalized LDP would lead to the end of
single-party dominance in Japan after 2009, this prediction has yet to
be realized. They further add that the days of strong Kōenkai are also
mostly over. If this is the case, then we should expect candidates to
run more nationalized campaigns and rely less on personal positions.

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item[\textbf{H2}]: Candidates are increasingly campaigning on a national
platform.
\end{itemize}
```

There are still some reasons to believe that this is not the case. The
above prediction has yet to be realized: the LDP returned to power in 2012 and
has remained in office since then. @catalinac18 provides empirical
evidence that parties became more unified after the 1994
electoral reform: the variance in within-party candidate positioning
decreased substantially after the reform. While these
results are compelling, they stop in 2009, when the DPJ won the election.
As highlighted above by @reed_etal12, the LDP changed its campaign style
between 2005 and 2009 to a more nationalized one. Therefore, what we still lack
is an understanding of how the LDP responded *after* its electoral defeat in 2009.
Given that the less decentralized campaign appears to be associated with
worse electoral results and a loss of power for the LDP, it is important
to see how the party responded to this defeat. The fundamental question
is whether it returned to a more decentralized campaign, leaving
more discretion to its candidates. This could potentially explain why the
party has not lost another election since returning to power in 2012.

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item[\textbf{H3}]: Within-party candidate dispersion increases post-2009.
\end{itemize}
```

## Model {#sec-model}

<!-- The previous model tries to answer this question by starting -->
<!-- from the assumption that party leader wants to win an election, and to -->
<!-- do so they have to maximize the total number of votes they receive in -->
<!-- each district. In this section, we will go over the previous explanations -->
<!-- that were proposed to answer this question, and see how do they compare -->
<!-- with the above model. -->

The setup is as follows. A national party $P$ seeks to gain as many
votes as possible in order to win an election. To achieve this, it has
to convince the local population across the whole country to i) turn out
on election day, and ii) vote for party $P$. To do this, the
party has resources that it can allocate across the different
constituencies to help promote certain candidates. Party $P$ also needs
to decide how much *discretion* its candidates can have in their campaigns.
For simplicity, we treat the allocation of resources as fixed in this
model and focus exclusively on the *centralization* choice of party $P$.

The problem of centralization is as follows. The leader ($L$) of
party $P$ does not know the local needs and issues of all the
constituencies.  Therefore, by granting little discretionary power to
the candidates ($C$) running for the party, he runs the risk of alienating
part of the electorate: his priorities might be far from those
of the local population in constituency $d$.

On the other hand, the party leader cannot delegate all power and
discretionary choices to the candidates. Doing so would be
suboptimal, as his preferences might not be aligned with
those of all the candidates. Delegating all of his power to
the local candidates thus runs the risk of letting these candidates run on
"unwanted platforms". The party still wants to campaign on a relatively
similar platform. Therefore, the choice is how far from the
party's national platform candidates can run.

The formalization is as follows. In this game, there is one party leader
$L$ and $N$ candidates, one per constituency $d \in \{1, \dots, N\}$.
The party leader $L$ has preferences represented by the utility function
$u_L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) = -\sum_{d=1}^{N} (x_d - \theta_d)^2$.
Here, $x_d$ represents the platform chosen by the candidate in
constituency $d$, and $\theta_d$ is the optimal point of constituency $d$.
Each constituency's optimal point is drawn i.i.d. from a distribution $F$,
$\theta_d \sim F$. The party leader does not observe the realization of
$\theta_d$, but he does know the distribution $F$.

The candidate in constituency $d$ has preferences represented by the utility function
$u_{C_d}(x_d, \theta_d, b) = -(x_d - \theta_d - b)^2$, where $x_d$ is
the candidate's platform, $\theta_d$ is the local optimal point, and $b$
is the bias, or disagreement, of the candidates with the party leader,
assumed to be common to all candidates.
Each candidate observes $\theta_d$ before choosing their own
platform $x_d$.

The game follows this timing: $L$ commits to a set of permitted platforms
$\mathcal{D}$; Nature draws $\theta_d$; candidate $d$ observes $\theta_d$;
candidate $d$ chooses $x_d \in \mathcal{D}$.

# Data

This project collects an original dataset using electoral bulletins
in Japan for the 2024 and 2026 lower house elections. The pipeline
is illustrated in @fig-pipeline. We first collected a sample of electoral
bulletins from 5 prefectures from the `go2senkyo` website. The website
compiles all the election bulletins across all districts, retrieved
from each prefecture's electoral commission. Once the files were
downloaded, we used the Claude API to identify the boundaries of each
candidate within the original file (see @sec-bulletin-ex in [the
Appendix](#sec-appendix) for an example).  Once the boundaries were identified,
we used pymupdf to segment the district file into separate
candidate files, such as @fig-candidate-example.  From there, we used
[Yomitoku](https://kotaro-kinoshita.github.io/yomitoku/en/), a Python
library optimized for Japanese text and documents, to parse and OCR the
individual bulletins. Yomitoku's models are all available on the Hugging
Face website.^[The maintainer's Hugging Face page is available at
[https://huggingface.co/KotaroKinoshita](https://huggingface.co/KotaroKinoshita).]

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 80%
%%| fig-cap: Pipeline of the project and future extension
%%| label: fig-pipeline
%%| file: flowchart.mmd
```

Once the parsing is done, we store the information in a Pandas dataframe.
Each candidate (row) has the following information attached:
1) the text of their election bulletin, 2) the number of paragraphs,
3) the number of headings, and 4) the total number of characters (including both
Kanji and Kana).

The main challenge is to find an efficient way to extract the content
of each candidate's bulletin. @fig-bulletin-ex shows an example of the
structure of the PDF files containing all the candidates within a district.
Some tests with Yomitoku on the complete PDF, like @fig-bulletin-ex,
introduced parsing errors: some text was attributed to the wrong
candidate, images and layout tended to have more influence on the parsing,
potentially due to their size relative to the text, and some aspects
of the layout tended to be overlooked by the parser.

@fig-candidate-example presents an example of an electoral bulletin for one
candidate.

![Political candidate in Aichi prefecture](../data/cleaned_bulletins/test/01_大西雅人_社民党.pdf){#fig-candidate-example width="80%"}

# Results {#sec-results}

This section presents some preliminary results from running the pipeline
described above on the sample of electoral bulletins. @fig-prelim-results
presents preliminary descriptive results. It plots the average number
of characters and paragraphs within parties. I used seaborn to make the
graphs. The horizontal bars are 95\% confidence intervals. We can see
that there is fair variation between parties on both of these metrics. It
is still too early to answer the question; these results serve primarily
to show what the dataset will allow us to do. After randomly selecting a
few bulletins and manually comparing them with the pymupdf cropping and
the Yomitoku OCR output, the extraction appears to work very well and is
quite accurate (above 95\%). Later on, I also want to perform structural
topic modeling [@roberts_etal13] using individual-level covariates of
the candidates and district-level covariates to study centralization
and how different characteristics are associated with the presence or
absence of certain topics. Finally, I used Claude Code to help me revise
and debug my code. I also used it to correct the grammar of this proposal,
but not to generate any of its text.

::: {#fig-prelim-results layout-ncol=2 fig-cap="Descriptive statistics about the electoral bulletins by political party. Points represent means, and horizontal bars are 95\% confidence intervals. The Liberal and Hoshuto parties do not have CIs, as they only have one candidate each in our sample."}
![Average number of characters](figures/avg_char.pdf){#fig-avg-char height="30%"}

![Average number of paragraphs](figures/avg_par.pdf){#fig-avg-par height="30%"}
:::

# Deliverables {#sec-deliverable}

For the rest of the semester, I will create a complete dataset covering the
2024 and 2026 lower house elections. I will try to finish the scraper that
will download all the electoral bulletins from each prefectural electoral
commission (week 1-2).^[If this does not work, I will complement it with,
or fall back on, the `go2senkyo` website.] Once they are downloaded, I can
run the pipeline on all of these bulletins and complement the preliminary
analyses with a larger sample of bulletins (week 3-4). Finally, I will
complete further analyses of the text and of party centralization (week 4-5).
